NASA SP-5110, prepared for NASA by Battelle Memorial Institute in 1972, opens: 'Some 10 years ago, Buehler and Wiley of the U.S. Naval Ordnance Laboratory developed a series of engineering alloys that possess a unique mechanical (shape) memory. The generic name of the series of alloys is 55-Nitinol, where Nitinol stands for Nickel Titanium Naval Ordnance Laboratory.' The allegation that Wright-Patterson-sponsored Battelle reports on nickel-titanium alloy from 1948-49 are missing from Air Force and Battelle archives is kept on this board as the allegation it is, and is unsupported by the federal literature opened here.

UAP Gerb's February 2024 investigation alleges that Battelle studied UAP material, likely a shape-memory alloy found at the Roswell crash site,, as documented by Jacques Vallee, and that Battelle worked with the Air Force from the 1950s to index UFO reports and quell public interest. The video cites retrievable records, including the Stork progress reports and Special Report No. 14.
John Brandenburg said on a 2025 podcast that there was a 1949 contract between Los Alamos and Battelle concerning nitinol, declassified by Battelle in the 1960s.

Jacques Vallee holds that the Robertson Panel of January 1953 was not briefed on the Pentacle proposals and that another group had already set the limits of what it could discuss. Jesse Michels has said on podcasts that the memo could not be raised around the panel, without citing a document for that.

The memorandum's date of 9 January 1953, its addressee, Miles E. Goll at Wright-Patterson, its Project Stork reference and its attribution to Battelle's H. C. Cross rest on the CUFON transcription and Vallee's copy; the board grades them Tier 2 and no signed original has been produced.

The board infers institutional continuity from Battelle's presence at the 1950s analysis of Air Force UFO data, at the 2022-24 specimen analysis, and in supplying MITRE's chief executive; the connections are documented and the significance is inference.

contested.text: The federal literature does not support a Battelle 1948-49 lineage for nitinol: the review Battelle wrote traces the alloy to the Naval Ordnance Laboratory around 1962 and cites no Battelle nickel-titanium work before 1968. The missing-reports allegation stands as an allegation, unsupported by the records opened.
The alleged Roswell connection rests on a coincidence of timing between the 1947 recovery, the claimed 1948-49 work and the absence of the reports; no document joins them.

The accounts disagree on the sponsor: the board's allegation names Wright-Patterson, while Brandenburg names Los Alamos, for the same alloy in the same period, and no contract record has been opened for either.

Jeremy Rys dated the laboratory's first nitinol discovery to 1954; the laboratory is right on the federal record but the date is not, since no opened document places any of its nitinol work before 1961.

The alleged 1947 crash specimen that Oak Ridge tested for AARO, a magnesium alloy and not nitinol, was assessed as terrestrial with no evidence of extraterrestrial origin, though neither AARO nor Oak Ridge could verify where it came from.
The Pentacle memorandum is known through a transcription and Vallee's copy; its dating and authorship are graded Tier 2 because no primary record of the memo is cited.

The Air Force's 1994 report attributed the Roswell debris to Project Mogul Flight No. 4, a balloon train launched from Alamogordo on 4 June 1947, which is the official explanation against the premise that shape-memory metal was recovered there.

The federal record, including a NASA review Battelle itself wrote, credits nitinol to the Naval Ordnance Laboratory, whose earliest cited nitinol report is dated 3 August 1961, and gives Battelle only a later subcontracting role.

record.text: NASA SP-5110, written for NASA by Battelle in 1972, opens by crediting Buehler and Wiley of the U.S. Naval Ordnance Laboratory with developing the shape-memory alloys about ten years earlier, and explains that Nitinol stands for Nickel Titanium Naval Ordnance Laboratory.

The earliest Naval Ordnance Laboratory nitinol report in SP-5110's references is NOLTR 61-75 of 3 August 1961, and US Patent 3,174,851 by Buehler and Wiley, assigned to the Secretary of the Navy, was filed on 1 December 1961 and granted on 23 March 1965.

NASA CR-1433 of September 1969 records that the nitinol was supplied by Buehler at the Naval Ordnance Laboratory and that Battelle, as subcontractor to Goodyear Aerospace, processed the basic rod; it calls the laboratory's work a recent discovery. NASA commissioned both reports.

Project Stork was Battelle's Air Force contract AF-19741, begun on 31 March 1952, to provide consultants, improve interrogation forms and analyse sighting reports for the Air Technical Intelligence Center at Wright-Patterson. Seven status reports are publicly available and the set is known to be incomplete; the contractor's name is struck out in most copies and typed in only one.

Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14 of 5 May 1955 analysed 2,199 objects and classed 434, or 19.7 per cent, as unknown. The report names no contractor anywhere on its face; the Battelle attribution rests on the Stork status reports, and AARO's history records that Battelle released it under ATIC's cover to keep its anonymity.

As transcribed by CUFON, the Pentacle memorandum proposes controlled experiments with observation posts in high-report areas, in which many types of aerial activity would be secretly and purposefully scheduled.

AARO contracted Oak Ridge National Laboratory, run by UT-Battelle, in 2022 to test a magnesium alloy specimen alleged to come from a 1947 crash. The laboratory assessed it as terrestrial and unable to act as a terahertz waveguide, while noting that its undocumented chain of custody leaves its origin unclear.

Battelle, founded in 1929 and based in Columbus, Ohio, runs or co-runs large federal laboratories: it holds the Pacific Northwest contract and co-operates Oak Ridge through UT-Battelle. Its executive Mark Peters became MITRE's chief executive on 3 September 2024.

summary.text: The allegation: Anthony Bragalia and others say Battelle's Wright-Patterson-sponsored nickel-titanium reports of 1948-49 are missing, and a 2024 video investigation by UAP Gerb argues, following Jacques Vallee's paper trail, that the alloy Battelle studied was likely material found at the Roswell crash site and is now called nitinol. No document connects Battelle's alloy work to Roswell directly.

The record set beside it: NASA's 1972 review, the Naval Ordnance Laboratory's 1961 technical report, the Navy's 1961 patent filing and a 1969 NASA contractor report, which together date and attribute the alloy.

Battelle's documented part in the Air Force UFO effort is real and separate: it held the Project Stork contract behind Blue Book Special Report No. 14, and a 1953 memorandum later attributed to its scientist H. C. Cross is known from a transcription. Separately, AARO contracted the Oak Ridge laboratory Battelle co-operates in 2022 to test an alleged 1947 crash specimen, reporting in 2024.

title: The Battelle nitinol allegation and the Naval Ordnance Laboratory record
